exploreAction.instruction: Read about how the French attempt was defeated less by rock than by disease - yellow fever and malaria - until the US effort took on the mosquitoes themselves, draining swamps and screening hospitals. Notice the engineering pivot: instead of a sea-level trench, a chain of locks lifting ships over the continental divide. Consider the human ledger of the project, the geopolitical deal that carved Panama from Colombia, and how a shortcut for trade reshaped the world's shipping lanes.

name: The Empire State Building (1931)
teaser: Raised at the start of the Great Depression, the world's tallest building went up in 410 days - with workers averaging four and a half floors a week. It was called the 'Empty State Building' for years.
byline: Built by the Starrett Brothers, New York

exploreAction.targetName: The Empire State Building's record-speed construction
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the construction's audacious speed - a skeleton of steel rising a floor every day, with materials arriving on a tight railway schedule - and the name's irony: completed in 1931, much of its office space sat empty for a decade. Notice the competition that drove it: a skyscraper race in New York in the 1920s and 30s. Consider what it meant to build the world's tallest tower as the economy collapsed, and how a symbol of confidence became a symbol of the Depression's excess.

name: Apartheid in South Africa (1948-1994)
teaser: A legal system built to keep racial separation permanent - with passbooks, homelands, and forced removals. It ended in 1994, not with a collapse of order but with a negotiated revolution and a truth commission.

exploreAction.targetName: How apartheid worked and how it ended
exploreAction.instruction: Read about apartheid's machinery - the Population Registration Act sorting everyone by race, the pass laws that controlled movement, and the homelands policy that stripped millions of citizenship. Notice the resistance it provoked: the Sharpeville massacre, the Soweto uprising, the international boycott movement, and the long imprisonment of Nelson Mandela. Consider the astonishing endgame - a negotiated transition and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission - and what a society chooses when it decides to tell the truth about itself instead of taking revenge.

name: The Moon Landing on Television (1969)
teaser: An estimated 600 million people watched the first moonwalk live - about a fifth of humanity. The transmission itself, from 380,000 kilometers away, was a technical feat on top of the flight.

exploreAction.targetName: How the moon landing reached television screens
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the broadcast engineering - the lunar module's low-power antenna, the tracking stations, and the 2.2 seconds of delay - and how the world gathered around screens at odd hours, with celebrations from London to Lagos. Notice the small drama: the first camera was mounted on the lander, and the famous first steps were nearly missed because it was switched on late. Consider what it meant for humanity to watch itself reach another world, and how live television made a shared experience of a single moment.

name: The Voynich Manuscript (c. 15th century)
teaser: A book written in a script no one can read, illustrated with plants that don't exist. Carbon dating confirms its age; every attempt at decipherment has failed - or been a hoax.

exploreAction.targetName: The Voynich Manuscript and its unsolved script
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the manuscript's features - its unreadable script, its botanical illustrations of imaginary plants, its astronomical diagrams - and the theories about it, from a lost language to a medieval hoax to an invented cipher. Notice what carbon dating and statistical analysis have established, and what they can't explain. Consider why a document that may be meaningless keeps pulling in codebreakers and cranks alike, and what our fascination with it says about the appeal of unsolved things.

name: Thomas Cromwell and Tudor Bureaucracy
teaser: The son of a blacksmith became Henry VIII's fixer, dissolving the monasteries and building the machinery of the modern English state. His fall was as swift as his rise - beheaded in 1540.

exploreAction.targetName: How Thomas Cromwell built the Tudor state
exploreAction.instruction: Read about how Cromwell rose from humble origins to engineer the break with Rome, dissolve the monasteries, and centralize royal power through Parliament and a professional bureaucracy. Notice the bureaucratic revolution hiding in his work: records, audits, and administrative machinery where medieval informality had ruled. Consider how the same skills that made him indispensable made him dangerous, and what his execution in 1540 - engineered by his rivals - reveals about the court politics of the age.

name: The First Great Wall (Qin Dynasty, 3rd century BCE)
teaser: The wall you picture today is mostly Ming dynasty. Qin Shi Huang's original was a series of rammed-earth fortifications linking older walls - built by hundreds of thousands of conscripts.

exploreAction.targetName: Qin Shi Huang's wall and the Ming wall that replaced it
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the first emperor's wall - earthen ramparts connecting older state walls to keep northern nomads out - and how later dynasties rebuilt it, with the surviving stone and brick version dating mostly to the Ming. Notice the human cost: conscript laborers built it at a terrible price, and legend says dead workers were buried in the fill. Consider how a defensive project that never fully stopped invaders still became a nation's symbol, and what the difference between the original and the tourist version tells you about history and myth.

name: Zheng He's Treasure Fleets (1405-1433)
teaser: A Chinese admiral commanded the largest wooden ships ever built and sailed them across the Indian Ocean decades before Columbus. Then China stopped, dismantled the fleet, and the era ended.

exploreAction.targetName: Zheng He's seven voyages across the Indian Ocean
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the treasure fleet's scale - ships reportedly far larger than anything Europeans built, with hundreds of vessels and tens of thousands of crew, sailing from China to East Africa. Notice the purpose: display, diplomacy, and tribute rather than conquest or colonization. Then read the counterintuitive ending: after Zheng He's death the voyages were stopped, the fleet burned, and China turned inward. Consider what it means when a state that had mastered the oceans chooses to abandon them, and why that choice still puzzles historians.

name: The Papal States (756-1870)
teaser: For over a thousand years, the pope ruled a swath of central Italy as a secular monarch - complete with armies, taxes, and wars. The unification of Italy ended it, and the pope became 'the prisoner of the Vatican.'

exploreAction.targetName: How the papacy ruled a state for a millennium
exploreAction.instruction: Read about how the donation of land in central Italy gave popes temporal power - popes who led armies, signed treaties, and taxed their subjects alongside their spiritual role. Notice the irony of the arrangement: the 'Donation of Constantine,' long used to justify papal lands, was later proven a forgery. Consider how the pope's loss of his state in 1870 changed the papacy's authority - stripped of armies, it gained moral stature - and what that says about power's strange accounting.

name: Paper Money in Yuan China (13th century)
teaser: Marco Polo was astonished: the Great Khan paid his armies with decorated paper that was 'worth as much as if it were pure gold.' It was the world's first government-backed paper currency.

exploreAction.instruction: Read about how the Yuan state issued paper notes, backed by the government's authority rather than metal reserves, and required their use - refusing them could cost you your life. Notice the warning it contains about money: when the treasury printed too much, inflation wrecked the system, and China returned to coin and, later, silver. Consider what Marco Polo's wonder reveals about how money is a story a society agrees to believe, and how the Yuan's lesson about overprinting is still taught in every economics class.

name: Venice's Fight Against the Water
teaser: Venice has been sinking for centuries - its wooden piles driven into mud, its groundwater pumped, its sea levels rising. Modern engineering now raises flood barriers from beneath the lagoon.
byline: The Republic of Venice and its successors

exploreAction.targetName: How Venice was built on water and keeps fighting it
exploreAction.instruction: Read about the engineering that lets a city sit on water - millions of wooden piles driven through mud to firm clay, buildings made light, and canals instead of streets - and the slow sinking caused partly by the pumping of groundwater and the weight of the city itself. Notice the modern answer, the MOSE flood barriers that rise from the lagoon floor. Consider what it means for a whole city to be a long-term experiment in defying its own geography.

name: The Siege of Syracuse (214-212 BCE)
teaser: A Roman army besieged a Greek city defended by Archimedes - whose war machines reportedly included a claw that lifted ships out of the water. The city fell anyway, and Archimedes died at a soldier's sword.

exploreAction.targetName: Archimedes's machines and the fall of Syracuse
exploreAction.instruction: Read about how the elderly Archimedes turned geometry into weapons - the stories, possibly exaggerated, of mirrors focusing sunlight on ships and a claw that grabbed Roman vessels by the prow. Notice that the city still fell after a two-year siege, and that Archimedes, absorbed in a diagram, was reportedly killed by a soldier who didn't know who he was. Consider why a single mind can delay but not decide a war, and how the death of the era's greatest scientist became part of the story of its greatest siege.

name: The Khmer Empire and Angkor (9th-15th century)
teaser: Angkor was one of the world's largest pre-industrial cities - a water-management civilization whose reservoirs and canals covered more land than the temples did. Its collapse may have been a water crisis.

exploreAction.targetName: Angkor's water systems and its fall
exploreAction.instruction: Read about how the Khmer engineered a city around water - massive reservoirs called barays, a network of canals, and the temple-mountain of Angkor Wat - and how archaeologists now read the landscape as one vast hydraulic machine. Notice the leading theory of the collapse: the water system, overtaxed by climate swings and overexpansion, became the city's undoing. Consider what it means that a civilization's masterpiece of water engineering may have been what broke it, and what that warns about infrastructure built at the edge of its limits.

name: The Maya City-States (c. 250-900 CE)
teaser: A civilization of dozens of rival city-states that built towering temples in the jungle, wrote books in a script we've only recently deciphered, and collapsed mysteriously around 900 CE.

exploreAction.targetName: Maya cities, writing, and the Classic collapse
exploreAction.instruction: Read about how the Maya built cities like Tikal and Calakmul with precise calendars, monumental architecture, and a full writing system - much of it now deciphered, revealing dynasties and wars. Notice the collapse: over a few generations, the great cities were abandoned, and scholars now point to a combination of drought, overpopulation, and intercity warfare. Consider how a civilization that knew enough astronomy to predict eclipses could not escape its own ecological limits, and what the Maya's slow, structural end - not a single catastrophe - says about resilience.

name: The Jesuits in Ming China (16th-17th century)
teaser: Jesuit missionaries reached the Ming court not with armies but with mathematics, clocks, and maps - and were appointed to run China's calendar. The encounter mixed wonder, suspicion, and influence.

exploreAction.targetName: Matteo Ricci's mission and the science exchange
exploreAction.instruction: Read about how Matteo Ricci learned Chinese, adopted Confucian dress, and impressed the court with European science - astronomy, cartography, and clocks - earning the Jesuits a place at the imperial court and responsibility for the calendar. Notice the cultural trading: Ricci translated Confucian classics to Europe while the Jesuits introduced Western astronomy to China. Consider what this exchange - conducted without conquest - reveals about how knowledge moves between civilizations, and why it ended as Europe's approach shifted.

name: The Day the Dinosaurs Died (66 million years ago)
teaser: An asteroid roughly 10 kilometers wide hit the Yucatan and ended 165 million years of dinosaur rule. The impact winter that followed also cleared the way for mammals - and, eventually, for us.

exploreAction.targetName: The Chicxulub impact and the K-Pg extinction
exploreAction.instruction: Read about how the impact hypothesis - an iridium layer found worldwide, then a buried crater under Mexico's coast - came to be accepted, and what the day itself looked like: a fireball, tsunamis, and years of dust that starved the planet of sunlight. Notice that some birds, our dinosaurs, survived. Consider how a chance cosmic event reset the course of life on Earth, and how a single day 66 million years ago is the reason your own existence is possible.

name: Joan of Arc (1412-1431)
teaser: A teenage farm girl convinced a prince she heard divine voices, led an army to break a siege, and was burned at the stake by the same church that canonized her 500 years later.

exploreAction.targetName: Joan of Arc's campaign and trial
exploreAction.instruction: Read how an illiterate 17-year-old turned the Hundred Years' War around in nine days at Orleans. Notice that her trial record survives in full - we have her exact words under questioning. Then decide what you think she actually believed: voices, or certainty.

name: The Printing Press (c. 1440)
teaser: Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type press made a book that took a scribe a year to copy in days. Europe went from a few thousand books to millions within a generation.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how movable metal type and an oil-based ink turned bookmaking into a factory process. Notice the 42-line Bible still being cited as one of the most beautiful printed objects ever made, then trace the shockwave: literacy, reformation, science.

name: The Fall of Constantinople (1453)
teaser: The Ottomans hauled ships overland on greased logs to outflank a city protected by sea. Its last emperor died fighting on the walls, and the ancient world's greatest city became Istanbul.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Mehmed II dragged 70 ships over a hill on rollers to break the Golden Horn chain - the move that shocked the defenders. Notice the double walls had held for a thousand years and what finally cracked them: cannons and a forgotten gate.

name: Columbus's First Voyage (1492)
teaser: He sailed west to find Japan, miscalculated the Earth's circumference, and hit islands he insisted were Asia. Three voyages later he still didn't know he'd found a new continent.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the log of the first crossing and notice the geography error that made it possible: he thought Asia was 3,000 miles west of Spain when it's really 12,000. Then weigh how the same voyage is remembered completely differently depending on who tells it.

name: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)
teaser: Two kingdoms split the unexplored world with a line drawn through the Atlantic - Spain got everything west of it, Portugal east. Brazil ended up on the wrong side, which is why Brazilians speak Portuguese.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a pope's ruling divided the planet along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Azores. Notice that no one knew what lay on either side, and how a later adjustment accidentally gave Portugal South America's biggest country.

name: Leonardo da Vinci's Notebooks (c. 1480-1519)
teaser: Roughly 7,000 surviving pages of mirror-writing, anatomy sketches, and flying machines. He designed a helicopter 400 years before flight and a parachute that worked when tested in 2000.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Leonardo wrote backwards from right to left, probably to keep rivals out - and why his 'lost' works only surfaced centuries later. Notice the anatomical drawings done from actual dissections, still admired by surgeons today.

name: The Spanish Inquisition (1478-1834)
teaser: Created to police converted Jews and Muslims, it ran for 356 years and burned about 1,500 people - a fraction of the number killed in the European witch panics it actually moderated.

exploreAction.targetName: How the Spanish Inquisition actually worked
exploreAction.instruction: Read past the myths to how the tribunal really functioned: manuals of procedure, evidence rules, even torture limits that rival kingdoms laughed at. Notice how a bureaucracy of fear outlasted every king who created it.

name: The Protestant Reformation (1517)
teaser: A monk nailed 95 complaints about indulgences to a church door, and within a generation half of Europe had split from Rome. The printing press made sure every word spread in weeks.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 95 Theses and notice how mundane most of them are - they're a professor's list of debate points, not a manifesto. Then trace how a local dispute became a continent-wide rupture because printed pamphlets traveled faster than any heresy trial could.

name: Magellan's Circumnavigation (1519-1522)
teaser: Magellan died in the Philippines, stabbed in a pointless skirmish. Of 270 men who sailed, 18 returned on one battered ship - the first people ever to cross every meridian on Earth.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the harrowing crossing of the Pacific - 98 days without fresh food, men eating leather and sawdust - and notice the fleet had already mutinied once. Then find the strange fact: the crew 'lost' a day crossing the date line and thought they'd broken the calendar.

name: The Aztec Capital Tenochtitlan (1325-1521)
teaser: Built on a lake with canals instead of streets, it had floating gardens, a 78,000-person market, and aqueducts. When the Spanish first saw it they called it the most beautiful city on Earth - then they destroyed it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a city on a swamp grew into one bigger than any in Europe, with causeways wide enough for eight horsemen. Notice the engineering: chinampas that produced up to seven harvests a year, and the aqueduct that brought fresh water from a volcano.

name: The Inca Road System (c. 1438-1533)
teaser: A 25,000-mile network across the Andes with rope bridges, stone stairways, and relay runners who moved messages faster than horses could in Europe. Sections of it are still walkable today.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a state without wheels or writing managed an empire the size of the Roman one, using khipu knots for records and chasqui runners on relay. Notice the roads were built to last - some stretches are so well set that not a stone has shifted in 500 years.

name: Copernicus's On the Revolutions (1543)
teaser: A cautious cleric proposed the Sun, not the Earth, at the center. He dedicated the book to the pope and died the year it printed - only 400 copies sold, and most readers thought it was about astronomy, not heresy.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Copernicus kept circular orbits (making his system barely simpler than Ptolemy's) and notice the book's own preface hedges that it's all hypothetical. Then see why it took a century and Kepler's ellipses to make it actually work.

name: The Ottoman Siege of Vienna (1529)
teaser: Suleiman the Magnificent's army reached the gates of Vienna and turned back after three weeks - mostly due to rain, mud, and disease. Europe called it a triumph; the Ottomans called it a reconnaissance.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how close the Ottomans actually came and why they left: winter, resupply failure, and a garrison that kept sallying out. Notice that the 'great victory' was really the weather's - and how the myth of Christian salvation shaped Austrian identity for centuries.

name: The Taj Mahal (1632-1653)
teaser: An emperor built a marble mausoleum for his favorite wife using 20,000 workers and 1,000 elephants. The stones change color with the light, and the four minarets lean outward so they'd fall away from the tomb in an earthquake.

exploreAction.targetName: The building of the Taj Mahal
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the white marble was hauled 400 kilometers and inlaid with 28 kinds of precious stone. Notice the optical trick: the central dome looks larger than it is because the surrounding elements shrink as they rise, and the calligraphy appears uniform though the letters are graded in size.

name: The English Civil War (1642-1651)
teaser: A king fought his own parliament, lost, and became the only British monarch ever publicly executed. For eleven years England was a republic - then it invited the dead king's son back.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a tax dispute over 'ship money' escalated into a war that killed 200,000 people in a nation of five million. Notice that the real argument - who rules, the crown or the people - kept erupting for another century until a compromise was built.

name: The Peace of Westphalia (1648)
teaser: A set of treaties ended thirty years of European religious war and invented the modern idea: that each ruler gets to decide their own state's religion, and no outside power interferes.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the war's peace conference took five years and produced no single document. Notice the quiet revolution inside: the pope's objections were ignored, and for the first time sovereign states, not a universal church, became the unit of Europe.

name: The Scientific Revolution (1543-1687)
teaser: In 150 years humanity went from 'because Aristotle said so' to calculus and gravity. The revolution's oddest heroes include a scientist who burned his hand off proving vacuums work.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a handful of thinkers replaced authority with experiment - from Vesalius dissecting bodies to Newton publishing in Latin for a tiny audience. Notice how much depended on new tools: telescopes, microscopes, and the printing press carrying arguments across borders.

name: The Tokugawa Shogunate (1603-1868)
teaser: Japan closed itself to the world for 250 years - no foreign ships, no emigration, executions for unauthorized contact. When it reopened, it modernized so fast it became a world power in one generation.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the shoguns froze society into four castes and kept peace by making every daimyo live in Edo every other year. Notice the paradox: the 'locked country' era produced Japan's most beloved culture - haiku, ukiyo-e, kabuki - precisely because war was banned.

name: The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648)
teaser: Europe's bloodiest religious war was fought over a Bohemian church that the emperor closed. By the end, some German regions had lost two-thirds of their people - and no one could remember what started it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a defenestration - literally throwing officials out a window - lit a war that pulled in most of Europe. Notice the war's most chilling invention: armies that fed themselves by looting, which made the suffering outlast the fighting.

name: The Great Fire of London (1666)
teaser: A bakery oven in Pudding Lane burned 13,000 houses and 87 churches in four days. Only six people died - but London was rebuilt in brick and stone, and the fire may have ended the plague that had been killing thousands.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a fire that destroyed the medieval city also killed off the black rat and its fleas - the plague had been running for a year. Notice the reconstruction rules that still shape London: no more thatch, no more overhanging timber, wider streets.

name: Newton's Principia (1687)
teaser: The book that invented physics was written in eighteen months after Newton had abandoned science for alchemy. Its laws of motion and gravity are still used to land spacecraft today.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Newton unified the moon and the apple under one law and why the book is famously hard - he wrote it in dense geometry on purpose, to keep out mathematicians who couldn't keep up. Notice he was sure light was particles; he was wrong, but wrong in a way that lasted 200 years.

name: The Glorious Revolution (1688)
teaser: England replaced its king with almost no bloodshed - James II simply fled. Parliament wrote the rules afterward, and every British monarch since has ruled only with parliament's blessing.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a Dutch prince invaded with a fleet larger than the Spanish Armada and met almost no resistance. Notice the twist: the revolution that ended absolute monarchy was barely a revolution - the king tripped on a tide schedule and left.

name: The Salem Witch Trials (1692)
teaser: Nineteen people were hanged in a Massachusetts village after teenage girls accused them of witchcraft. A year later the courts admitted it was a mistake - the accusers had been caught in a circle of gossip and fear.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the crisis began with a slave's tales of voodoo and spread through a village riven by land disputes. Notice the court accepted 'spectral evidence' - testimony about ghosts - until the governor's own wife was accused, and then suddenly stopped.

name: Peter the Great's Reforms (1689-1725)
teaser: A giant tsar who learned shipbuilding in Dutch shipyards taxed beards, forced nobles to shave, and moved Russia's capital to a swamp he built with 30,000 forced laborers - to make Russia a European power.

exploreAction.targetName: Peter the Great's modernization of Russia
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Peter went west disguised as a common carpenter to learn shipbuilding himself. Notice the strange detail: he personally helped cut off nobles' beards at parties, and his beard tax is one of history's most effective - and most humiliating - revenue schemes.

name: The Battle of Poltava (1709)
teaser: Russia's first great military victory broke the Swedish empire and made Russia a power. Peter celebrated by giving captured Swedish generals a feast - while his own soldiers watched from the gallows he'd built for deserters.
byline: Peter the Great vs. Charles XII

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Charles XII of Sweden, wounded and commanding from a stretcher, was crushed by a Russian army twice his size. Notice what the battle decided: the Baltic forever left Swedish hands and Russia took its place as the region's heavyweight.

name: The South Sea Bubble (1720)
teaser: A company that existed to trade with a place it had no business in saw its shares rise 1,000% in a year, then collapse. Half of England's elite had invested - including the king, the chancellor, and Isaac Newton, who lost 20,000 pounds.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a firm that did almost no actual trade became the most valuable in Britain through rumor and bribes. Notice Isaac Newton's famous double loss: he sold early with a profit, bought back at the top, and lost it all - the smartest man in England caught by the same fever as everyone else.

name: The Enlightenment (c. 1685-1815)
teaser: A century of thinkers argued that reason, not kings or priests, should rule. Their ideas - rights, checks and balances, free speech - are still the operating system of modern democracies.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a small circle of Parisian philosophers, publishing books banned by the king, reshaped the Western mind. Notice the contradiction at the heart of it: many Enlightenment stars were patronized by the same absolute monarchs whose power their ideas dissolved.

name: The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-1748)
teaser: Half of Europe invaded Austria because its new ruler was a woman. Maria Theresa kept her throne, made her husband co-emperor, and named her second son Joseph - the future emperor - as she fought.

exploreAction.targetName: The War of the Austrian Succession
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Maria Theresa, pregnant and outnumbered, rallied the Hungarian nobles to defend a crown that European law said a woman couldn't hold. Notice the war's real casualty: the fiction that treaties meant anything, as everyone switched sides mid-conflict.

name: The Seven Years' War (1756-1763)
teaser: Fought on five continents, it's often called the first true world war - and it ended with Britain taking Canada, India, and world dominance from France. Its debts then provoked a tax that started another war.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a dispute over an Ohio river valley fort escalated into a global conflict from India to the Caribbean. Notice the war's secret: Britain won at sea while losing most of the land battles, and the peace treaty redrew half the world map.

name: Captain Cook's First Voyage (1768-1771)
teaser: Sailing to observe Venus cross the sun, Cook instead charted New Zealand and eastern Australia with maps so good some were used into the 1990s. His secret: fresh food that stopped scurvy.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Cook reached Australia by accident - his secret orders were to find the southern continent, and he proved it didn't exist. Notice his obsessive anti-scurvy diet of sauerkraut and citrus, the discovery that let his crew survive voyages that killed others.

name: The Boston Tea Party (1773)
teaser: Colonists dressed as Mohawk Indians dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston harbor to protest a tax cut - the tea was actually cheaper, but they objected to the principle. Britain responded by closing the port.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the protest was about the right to choose, not the price - the tea was cheaper with the tax than without it. Notice the detail that ruined the scheme: the tide was out, so the tea piled up in the harbor and had to be raked away for days.

name: The Declaration of Independence (1776)
teaser: Written in seventeen days by a quiet Virginia lawyer, its opening lines became the most quoted political words in history. Britain's official response was to hire 30,000 German soldiers to crush it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the famous second paragraph and notice it's an argument from rights, not a list of taxes - Jefferson aimed at the heart of monarchy itself. Then find the detail that stings: the same document that declared all men equal was signed by men who enslaved people.

name: The Battle of Saratoga (1777)
teaser: The American victory that convinced France to join the war - without French money, ships, and soldiers, the rebellion probably collapses. A British general's plan to split New England in two failed in the autumn mud.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a British army marching south from Canada with 600 wagons of luxury supplies got bogged down in New York woods. Notice the turning point: Benedict Arnold, later America's most famous traitor, commanded the charge that won the day.

name: The Constitution of the United States (1787)
teaser: Fifty-five delegates met in secret to design a government, argued for four months, and produced the world's oldest written constitution still in force. It was ratified by the narrowest of margins.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the delegates compromised on everything from representation to slavery to make the document pass. Notice the genius and the original sin in one sentence: the word 'slave' never appears, yet the counting of three-fifths of enslaved people for representation is written in.

name: The French Revolution (1789-1799)
teaser: A famine, a bankrupt crown, and a bread riot turned into a decade that executed a king, abolished the calendar, and redrew Europe. The revolutionaries' slogan - liberty, equality, fraternity - outlived every one of them.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a failed harvest and empty treasury pushed France past the tipping point, then watch the spiral: a king who fled in disguise, a war that radicalized everything, and the guillotine claiming the revolutionaries themselves. Notice that the modern left-right political divide was born in one French assembly vote.

name: The Storming of the Bastille (1789)
teaser: A mob seized a fortress holding seven prisoners - a forger, four aristocrats, and a madman. The crowd wanted gunpowder, not freedom, but the fall of the Bastille became the symbol of the revolution.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the 'tyranny's prison' the mob liberated was actually being demolished anyway, and held almost nobody. Notice the day's real consequence: the king, hearing the news, asked 'is it a revolt?' and was told, 'No sire, it is a revolution.'

name: The Haitian Revolution (1791-1804)
teaser: The only successful slave revolt in history: enslaved people defeated three empires and founded the world's first Black republic. Haiti then had to pay France for its own freedom - a debt that crippled it for a century.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Toussaint Louverture, a former slave who read Caesar, outgeneraled French, British, and Spanish armies. Notice the cruelty of the aftermath: France forced the new nation to pay 150 million francs in compensation for the 'lost property' - the slaves - the revolution had freed.

name: The Reign of Terror (1793-1794)
teaser: In less than a year, revolutionary tribunals guillotined 17,000 people - including the revolutionaries who started it. The Terror ended only when its own leader was executed, in a law he had written.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a committee of public safety turned suspicion itself into a crime, and how the guillotine became the most efficient executioner in history - 300 in one Paris month alone. Notice Robespierre's end: the law he passed to speed up trials was used on him the same day.

name: Napoleon's Egyptian Campaign (1798-1801)
teaser: Napoleon invaded Egypt to cut Britain's route to India and instead found the Rosetta Stone, inspired a science institute, and lost his fleet to Nelson. He abandoned his army and slipped home to seize power.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Napoleon brought 167 scientists along with 40,000 soldiers - the campaign that birthed Egyptology. Notice the absurd detail: he once escaped captivity disguised as a Bedouin, and his soldiers' discovery of the Rosetta Stone made the failed invasion an intellectual triumph.

name: The Rosetta Stone Found (1799)
teaser: A slab of black basalt with the same decree in three scripts became the key to reading hieroglyphs after 1,500 years of silence. The soldier who found it didn't know he'd grabbed history's most valuable rock.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery and decipherment of the Rosetta Stone
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the stone, written in hieroglyphs, demotic, and Greek, let scholars compare scripts line by line. Notice the twenty-year puzzle: even with the Greek version, hieroglyphs stayed unreadable until a young Frenchman realized they were partly phonetic - and his rival in England died claiming credit.

name: The Louisiana Purchase (1803)
teaser: America bought 828,000 square miles - a third of the country - from France for 15 million dollars, about 3 cents an acre. Napoleon sold it to fund a war he was losing.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Jefferson, a strict constitutionalist, bought land the Constitution didn't mention, doubling his country with one stroke of a pen. Notice the irony: he'd sent explorers to claim the territory for America a year before he legally owned it.

name: The Battle of Trafalgar (1805)
teaser: Nelson destroyed a combined French-Spanish fleet without losing a single ship, then was shot dead on his own deck. Britain's naval supremacy lasted a century and stopped Napoleon from ever invading.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Nelson broke the line in two columns against standard tactics and paid with his life - his last signal before dying was 'England expects every man will do his duty.' Notice the outcome's size: Britain kept control of the seas for the next hundred years.

name: The Battle of Austerlitz (1805)
teaser: Napoleon's masterpiece: he let the enemy occupy a strong position, then crushed the Allied center when they abandoned it. The battle ended the Holy Roman Empire and is still taught in war colleges as a perfect trap.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Napoleon deliberately weakened his right flank to lure the Allies down from the heights, then struck their exposed center. Notice the cold detail: he waited until the sun rose over the frozen lakes so the ice would hold his charges - and the story that thousands of Russians drowned breaking through it.

name: The Abolition of the Slave Trade (1807)
teaser: Britain outlawed the transatlantic slave trade after a 20-year campaign built on sugar boycotts and a black ex-slave's memoir. The Royal Navy then spent 60 years policing the ban - the largest anti-slavery operation in history.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a small group of abolitionists, armed with one former slave's testimony and a sugar boycott, overturned one of the most profitable industries on Earth. Notice the campaign tactic that was brand new: moral consumer choice - 'buy free-grown sugar' - the ancestor of today's ethical shopping.

name: The Battle of Waterloo (1815)
teaser: Napoleon's final defeat came after a day of savage fighting that broke the flower of two armies. He fled to Paris, abdicated, and died six years later on a British island - saying 'Waterloo' was the most beautiful word in history.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a rain-soaked night changed everything - the mud delayed Napoleon's attack, giving the Prussians time to arrive. Notice the razor's edge: Wellington said it was 'the nearest run thing you ever saw in your life,' a battle decided in the last hour.

name: Simón Bolívar (1783-1830)
teaser: A Venezuelan aristocrat liberated five nations from Spain, dreamed of a united South America, and died saying his work was 'plowing the sea.' His name became a country; his dream never did.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a rich man who'd been to Europe and seen Napoleon give up a life of leisure to march an army across the Andes - twice - over passes higher than any Alps. Notice the dream he died with: Gran Colombia, a single Spanish-speaking superstate, which fractured within a decade.

name: The Opium Wars (1839-1860)
teaser: Britain fought China to keep selling opium after China tried to ban it. The wars ended with Hong Kong ceded, ports opened, and Britain calling the result 'free trade.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the world's largest economy was defeated by a nation three times smaller because of a drug Britain's government had banned at home but forced on China at gunpoint. Notice the diplomatic detail: Britain went to war claiming the right to sell the drug, and the peace treaty is still called 'unequal' in China.

name: The Great Irish Famine (1845-1852)
teaser: A potato blight that could have been managed became a catastrophe: a million starved, a million fled, and food exports continued throughout - Ireland kept shipping grain to England while its people died.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how one fungus destroyed the crop that two-thirds of Ireland's poor lived on, and how relief policy made it worse - workhouses, no aid for the landless, and grain still leaving Irish ports. Notice the demographic scar: Ireland's population has never returned to pre-famine levels, 175 years later.

name: The California Gold Rush (1848-1855)
teaser: A single nugget found at a sawmill drew 300,000 people to California in five years. San Francisco grew from 1,000 to 25,000 in a year, and the state skipped territoryhood - it went straight to statehood.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the first gold strike was kept secret for months until a merchant ran through the streets waving a bottle of gold dust. Notice the forgotten millions: the rush wrecked California's native peoples, who had lived there for millennia, in the deadliest chapter of the state's history.

name: The Revolutions of 1848
teaser: In one year, revolution toppled kings from Paris to Vienna to Budapest. Within three years almost all of them were back - but the ideas, from voting to workers' rights, never went away.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a Paris street protest against election rules spread like a rumor through a continent wired with new telegraphs and printed pamphlets. Notice the pattern that would repeat: the revolutions won fast, then fractured between moderates and radicals, letting the old monarchies walk back in.

name: The Crimean War (1853-1856)
teaser: A war over who'd protect holy sites in Palestine became the first 'modern' war - railroads, telegraphs, war correspondents, and the work of Florence Nightingale. It also produced the Charge of the Light Brigade, an attack ordered by mistake.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a religious squabble escalated into a war that killed 600,000 - most from disease, not battle. Notice the absurd charge: the Light Brigade rode into the wrong valley because orders got scrambled, and 200 of 600 came back; the poem and the war correspondents made Britain watch its own disaster in real time.

name: The Indian Rebellion of 1857
teaser: A mutiny began when Indian soldiers refused to bite cartridges greased with animal fat - which rumor said was cow and pig. It ended the East India Company and made Queen Victoria empress of a direct colony.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a single ammunition detail - cartridges you bit open, greased with fat sacred to both Hindus and Muslims - united the Indian army in revolt. Notice the aftermath's scale: the British government dissolved the world's most powerful corporation and took India directly for the crown.

name: Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859)
teaser: A quiet naturalist's book about pigeons and barnacles argued that species change by natural selection. The first printing of 1,250 sold out on publication day; the debate it started hasn't ended.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Darwin built his argument from humble evidence - pigeon breeding, barnacles, island finches - rather than grand pronouncements, and how he sat on it for twenty years, terrified of the reaction. Notice the book never says humans descended from apes; it says it as carefully as possible without saying it.

name: The Meiji Restoration (1868)
teaser: Japan overthrew 250 years of shogun rule in weeks, then industrialized at a pace no country has matched - from samurai swords to battleships in forty years. The emperor went from hidden god to uniformed commander.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a group of young samurai, the very class being abolished, dismantled feudalism and remade Japan in a generation. Notice the paradox that made it work: the slogan was 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians,' yet they used Western technology, law, and arms to avoid being colonized like their neighbors.

name: The Suez Canal Opens (1869)
teaser: A ditch 120 miles long cut through desert, linking the Mediterranean and Red Seas and shaving 4,000 miles off the voyage to India. It was dug by hand - 1.5 million people, mostly forced labor.

exploreAction.targetName: The building of the Suez Canal
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the canal was built with 1.5 million workers over ten years, mostly under the khedive's forced-labor policy that France's press hailed as progress. Notice the geopolitical echo: the canal's debts bankrupted Egypt, which invited Britain in - and Britain stayed for seventy years.

name: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863)
teaser: Lincoln freed enslaved people in the Confederate states - where he had no power - and kept slavery legal in Union states where he did. Yet it transformed the war and the world: after it, every Union victory was a blow for freedom.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the document's careful legal language and notice what it actually did: declared the rebels' slaves free, let Black men enlist, and dared Europe to keep backing the Confederacy. It freed no one on day one - but it meant the war could never end with slavery intact.

name: The Gettysburg Address (1863)
teaser: Two minutes after a two-hour oration, Lincoln's 272 words redefined America as a nation dedicated to an idea. The speech was so short the photographer missed it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the 272 words and notice what Lincoln did: he never mentions the battle, slavery, or even victory. Instead he quietly rewrites the Declaration - 'all men are created equal' - into the nation's founding principle, a century before it was made real.

name: The Transcontinental Railroad (1869)
teaser: Two crews laid 1,900 miles of track toward each other across deserts and mountains, meeting at a gold spike. The Chinese workers who built the hardest section were paid less and buried in the trackbed.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how crews laid up to ten miles of track in one day and how the route's most dangerous work - granite tunnels through the Sierra Nevada - was done by Chinese laborers who were lowered in baskets to drill and blast. Notice the finish line ceremony: a golden spike driven where the rails met, with the workers who built it standing outside the frame.

name: The Franco-Prussian War (1870-1871)
teaser: A forged telegram insulting the French ambassador let Prussia provoke France into a war it won in six weeks. The peace treaty created the German Empire - in Versailles' Hall of Mirrors - and took Alsace, fueling revenge for 44 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Bismarck edited a king's telegram to sound insulting, knowing France would declare war, and how a French emperor surrounded at Sedan surrendered his entire army. Notice the seed of both world wars: a humiliated France and a suddenly united, militarized Germany facing each other over Alsace-Lorraine.

name: The Berlin Conference (1884-1885)
teaser: Fourteen European states met to divide Africa among themselves - no African was invited. In twenty years the map went from a few coastal forts to a continent carved into colonies with ruler-drawn straight lines.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Europeans, who controlled maybe 10% of Africa at the time, partitioned the remaining 90% on paper in ninety days. Notice the legacy in every straight border on modern maps of Africa - and how the conference's 'effective occupation' rule forced the scramble that followed.

name: The Eiffel Tower (1889)
teaser: Built as a temporary entrance arch for a world's fair, Paris's leading artists called it a 'hated column of bolted metal' and demanded its removal. It was saved by radio - its height made it the perfect antenna.

exploreAction.targetName: The building of the Eiffel Tower
exploreAction.instruction: Read how 18,000 iron pieces and 2.5 million rivets were assembled in two years, and how the tower was designed to sway only 6-7 centimeters in the wind. Notice the tower's second life: condemned after the fair, it survived because Eiffel put a radio lab at the top - the first wireless link across the Atlantic.

name: The Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901)
teaser: Chinese fighters, called Boxers for their martial-arts drills, besieged the foreign legations in Beijing for 55 days, believing their rituals made them bulletproof. Eight foreign armies marched in to lift the siege and extract a crushing indemnity.
byline: The Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a secret society armed with swords and faith took on eight empires, and how bullets did, in fact, find them. Notice the aftermath's weight: the foreign powers demanded 450 million taels in reparations - a sum China was still paying interest on half a century later.

name: The Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905)
teaser: Japan stunned the world by defeating a European empire - the first time an Asian power won a modern war. Russia's defeat sparked its 1905 revolution, and Japan's victory shifted the balance of power toward a rising East.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Japan attacked without declaring war, sank Russia's fleet in two battles, and forced a European empire to sue for peace. Notice the global ripple: colonized peoples from India to Egypt read the result as proof that empires could fall, and Lenin called the 1905 unrest 'the dress rehearsal' for 1917.

name: Einstein's Miracle Year (1905)
teaser: A 26-year-old patent clerk published four papers that founded modern physics - including E=mc2 - in a single year, while working a day job. He wasn't a professor, couldn't get a PhD supervisor, and had almost no library access.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Einstein, working alone at a patent office, resolved the century-old mystery of the photoelectric effect and upended time itself with special relativity. Notice the paper that won him the Nobel - not relativity, but the photoelectric effect - and how he'd later call his cosmological constant his 'biggest blunder.'

name: The Wright Brothers' First Flight (1903)
teaser: Two bicycle mechanics from Ohio flew 120 feet in 12 seconds - the first powered, controlled, heavier-than-air flight. Five spectators showed up; the local newspaper got the story wrong and called it a hoax.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the brothers solved what glider pioneers couldn't: control, through wing-warping and a rudder - discovered in a wind tunnel they built from a bicycle shop. Notice that the world took four more years to believe it, and that the Wrights' first customer was the US Army, which signed up to inspect a plane in 1908.

name: The San Francisco Earthquake (1906)
teaser: A 7.9 quake and the fires it started destroyed 80% of the city and killed over 3,000. The official death toll was 478 - undercounted for decades to protect the real estate market.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the quake lasted less than a minute but the fires raged for four days - fed by broken gas mains and a water system that failed at the hydrants. Notice the cover-up: officials insisted rebuilding was safe and the death count was low, while bodies were burned in the ruins and the real toll only surfaced decades later.

name: The Sinking of the Titanic (1912)
teaser: The 'unsinkable' ship went down on its maiden voyage after hitting an iceberg that lookouts spotted too late. It carried lifeboats for barely half its passengers - but the most expensive people got seats first.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the ship had exactly enough lifeboats to satisfy 1912 law - a law written for ships a quarter the size - and how the crew loaded boats partly empty, then sealed the third-class gates. Notice the statistic that tells the class story: 60% of first class survived, 25% of steerage.

name: The Assassination at Sarajevo (1914)
teaser: A teenager with a sandwich and a lucky street corner shot the heir to the Austrian throne, and within five weeks Europe was at war. The first assassination attempt failed - the bomb missed - but Gavrilo Princip got a second chance at a deli.

exploreAction.instruction: Read the chain of absurdities: the archduke's driver took a wrong turn onto the street where Princip was eating a sandwich. Notice how the assassination was the excuse, not the cause - the alliances, arms race, and rivalries had built the powder keg for a decade.

name: The Christmas Truce (1914)
teaser: On the first Christmas of World War I, soldiers on both sides climbed out of the trenches, exchanged gifts, sang carols, and played football in no-man's-land. The generals were horrified and made sure it never happened again.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how an estimated 100,000 men took part in unofficial ceasefires along the Western Front, burying their dead together and trading cigarettes for plum puddings. Notice the aftermath: commanders rotated units and ordered artillery barrages on Christmas to guarantee no repeat - the war's machinery learned from its men's mercy.

name: The Battle of Verdun (1916)
teaser: Ten months of fighting over a few square miles of French forts cost 700,000 casualties - the longest battle of World War I. The French held, and 'they shall not pass' became their rallying cry.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Germany's plan was not to break through but to bleed France dry - 'bleed them white' - by attacking a fortress France couldn't abandon. Notice the supply line that became legend: a single road, the Sacred Way, keeping the army fed while shells fell on the only route in.

name: The Russian Revolution (1917)
teaser: In eight months, strikes and mutinies toppled the tsar, then a second revolution in October handed power to Lenin's Bolsheviks - a coup by a minority party that expected a quick world revolution that never came.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the revolution began with bread lines and women textile workers striking on International Women's Day, and how the tsar's own soldiers refused to fire. Notice the smallest detail of the October coup: the 'storming of the Winter Palace' that became myth was nearly bloodless - the cruiser Aurora fired blanks, and most of the garrison was asleep.

name: The Treaty of Versailles (1919)
teaser: The peace that ended World War I assigned blame, demanded impossible reparations, and drew borders that ignored how people actually lived. Twenty years later, exactly the resentments it created launched a second world war.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Big Four - led by a French premier who wanted Germany's industry moved to France - wrote the treaty in six months, without any German at the table. Notice the detail that poisoned it: the 'war guilt' clause, forcing Germany to admit sole responsibility, which every German politician used as a grievance for two decades.

name: The Spanish Flu (1918-1920)
teaser: The deadliest pandemic in modern history killed 50 million people - more than the world war that spawned it - and then vanished almost as fast as it came. It was called Spanish only because Spain, neutral in the war, was the first to report it honestly.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a flu that mostly killed healthy young adults - the exact opposite of normal flu - raced through armies, ships, and cities in three waves. Notice the modern echo: masks, lockdowns, and second waves all happened in 1918, and the virus's descendants still circulate in the flu shots you get today.

name: Tutankhamun's Tomb Found (1922)
teaser: The only royal tomb in Egypt's Valley of the Kings found intact, stuffed with 5,000 objects - including a solid-gold death mask. The young king, dead at 19, was so minor that his tomb was forgotten for 3,000 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Carter's sponsor, Lord Carnarvon, was about to quit after five fruitless years - then a water boy found a step cut into the rock. Notice the irony that made the tomb priceless: Tutankhamun was an unremarkable boy-king, so his funeral goods were never looted, making them the best record of ancient Egyptian wealth ever found.

name: The Great Depression (1929-1939)
teaser: A stock market crash turned into a decade of global collapse: one in four American workers unemployed, banks failing by the thousand, and dust storms choking the farm belt. It ended only when rearmament rebuilt the economy.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the crash of 1929 was the symptom, not the cause - a decade of borrowing, overproduction, and a banking system with no safety net turned a market correction into a world depression. Notice how long it really lasted: by 1939 US unemployment was still 17%, and only wartime spending ended it.

name: Gandhi's Salt March (1930)
teaser: Gandhi and 78 followers walked 240 miles to the sea to make salt - breaking a British tax on a mineral everyone needed. Tens of thousands joined; Gandhi was arrested, and the image of a thin man picking up salt shook an empire.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Gandhi chose salt because it was the one tax that touched every Indian - rich and poor, Hindu and Muslim - and how the march was choreographed for the world's cameras. Notice the power of the gesture: no violence, no weapons, just millions breaking an unjust law at once, and the empire didn't know how to answer.

name: The New Deal (1933-1938)
teaser: In his first hundred days, Franklin Roosevelt created agencies that put millions to work building dams, parks, and post offices - and installed the safety net America still uses. His own party hated much of it; the Supreme Court struck parts of it down.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a president who could barely walk (polio had taken his legs, hidden from the cameras) remade the federal government's role in a single term. Notice the legacy hiding in plain sight: Social Security, the FDIC insurance on your bank deposits, and the 40-hour workweek all date to this program.

name: The Hindenburg Disaster (1937)
teaser: The largest flying machine ever built - a 245-meter hydrogen airship - burned in 34 seconds on a landing field in New Jersey. Thirty-six people died, and the age of passenger airships ended overnight.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the airship was filled with hydrogen because America refused to sell helium to Nazi Germany, and how the disaster's radio broadcast - a reporter sobbing 'oh, the humanity' - became one of the most famous recordings ever made. Notice the mystery: no one has conclusively proven what ignited it, and the leading theories include static, a spark, or sabotage.

name: Kristallnacht (1938)
teaser: A night of state-organized attacks on Jewish homes, synagogues, and businesses across Germany and Austria. The 'Night of Broken Glass' was presented as a spontaneous outburst - it was planned, and it was the point of no return.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a diplomat's assassination in Paris was used as the pretext for a night of coordinated violence, and how the state then fined the Jewish community one billion marks for the damage and confiscated insurance payouts. Notice the tipping point: after this night, emigration became desperate and the path to the Holocaust opened.

name: The Battle of Britain (1940)
teaser: The first battle ever fought entirely in the air: for four months, a few hundred RAF pilots held off the Luftwaffe, forcing Hitler to abandon his invasion. Churchill's tribute - 'never was so much owed by so many to so few' - made them immortal.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the RAF's secret weapon was a radar chain the Germans didn't understand, letting Spitfires and Hurricanes wait on the ground until the bombers committed. Notice the decision that saved Britain: the Luftwaffe switched from airfields to bombing London in September, giving the RAF the breathing room it needed.

name: The Attack on Pearl Harbor (1941)
teaser: In two hours, Japanese carrier aircraft sank or damaged 19 US ships and killed 2,400 Americans. The next day America declared war - and Japan's gamble of a knockout blow instead guaranteed a long war it could not win.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the attack came from 350 aircraft launched off six carriers that had crossed 4,000 miles undetected, and how American radar actually saw them coming - the operator was told to ignore the blips. Notice the outcome the attackers miscalculated: not one US carrier was in port, and the oil tanks they left standing fueled the Pacific war America won.

name: The Manhattan Project (1942-1945)
teaser: 130,000 people worked in secret for three years to build a bomb the size of a small car that could level a city. Most had no idea what they were building - their bosses told them it was for 'the project.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the project hid three cities in the desert and mountains, how Enrico Fermi built the first chain reaction in a squash court, and how the scientists who built the bomb later petitioned against using it. Notice the scale of the secret: Congress was never told the cost, and the vice president only learned of it after the president died.

name: The Battle of Stalingrad (1942-1943)
teaser: A city on the Volga became a meat grinder where soldiers survived an average of 24 hours. After five months, the German Sixth Army - 300,000 men - was surrounded and destroyed, the war's hinge.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a battle fought room-to-room in a ruined factory city broke the myth of German invincibility, and how the Soviets held at any cost - snipers, rats, and temperatures of -30 degrees. Notice the turning point detail: the commander who ordered 'not one step back' chose a position from which he couldn't retreat either.

name: D-Day (1944)
teaser: 156,000 Allied soldiers landed on five Normandy beaches on one day, under the largest naval invasion ever mounted. By nightfall the beachhead was only a few miles deep, but it was unbreakable - and within a year Hitler was dead.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the invasion was a triumph of deception - a fake army of inflatable tanks pinned German divisions to the wrong coast - and how the first wave took 90% casualties on some beaches. Notice the numbers: 5,000 ships, 11,000 aircraft, and a plan rehearsed for a year, all riding on a 24-hour weather forecast.

name: The Liberation of Auschwitz (1945)
teaser: Soviet soldiers arrived to find 7,000 starving prisoners and the machinery of a death factory - the largest of the Nazi camps, where over a million people were murdered, most within hours of arrival.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the camp's SS guards fled days before, destroying records but leaving the evidence - mountains of shoes, hair, and spectacles, and the gas chambers and crematoria built to process thousands a day. Notice the date: January 27, now International Holocaust Remembrance Day, when the world finally saw what industrial murder looked like.

name: The Hiroshima Bombing (1945)
teaser: A single bomb nicknamed 'Little Boy' killed roughly 100,000 people in seconds and ended World War II days later. It also opened the age where one nation could destroy a city with one aircraft.
byline: The United States Army Air Forces

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a B-29 named Enola Gay dropped a bomb the size of a torpedo that released more energy than all the explosives of the war combined. Notice the debate that still runs: whether the bomb shortened the war or was primarily a warning to the Soviet Union - and how the survivors, the hibakusha, carried both the scars and the testimony.

name: The United Nations Charter (1945)
teaser: Fifty-one nations signed a charter in San Francisco to 'save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.' The UN has never ended war, but it has given the world its only universal forum - and its flag flies over more capitals than any other.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the charter was written while the war was still being won, with the five victors writing themselves permanent vetoes. Notice the document's bet: that great powers could be persuaded to talk instead of fight - a bet that has held, barely, for eighty years.

name: The Nuremberg Trials (1945-1946)
teaser: For the first time, leaders of a defeated nation were held in open court for crimes against peace, war crimes, and a new category: crimes against humanity. Twelve of twenty-two were sentenced to death.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the trials put thousands of documents and testimonies into evidence - including the Nazis' own meticulous records - and how 'I was only following orders' failed as a defense. Notice the invention that outlived the court: the principle that individuals, not just states, can be guilty of crimes under international law.

name: The Partition of India (1947)
teaser: When Britain left, the subcontinent was split into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan in six weeks. Ten million people crossed borders in both directions, and up to two million died in the violence.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a British civil servant drew borders he'd never visited, using census data and an atlas, and how the new lines split villages, railways, and families. Notice the most painful detail: the Radcliffe Line was announced two days after independence, so no one knew which side of the border they were on when the killing began.

name: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
teaser: Drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, thirty articles declare rights for everyone - no exceptions. It's the most translated document in history, in over 500 languages.

exploreAction.targetName: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the declaration was written in two years by people from every continent and legal tradition, after the world had just witnessed what happens when rights are denied. Notice its quiet radicalism: article 1 says we are all born free and equal in dignity - a sentence no empire, church, or state had ever officially endorsed before.

name: The Berlin Airlift (1948-1949)
teaser: When the Soviets blockaded West Berlin, the Allies flew in everything - coal, milk, even a power plant - in 277,000 flights over 11 months. The city of two million never starved, and the blockade was broken without a shot.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the airlift was a logistical miracle - a plane landing every 90 seconds at its peak, with crews flying candy drops for children. Notice what it proved: that a city could be supplied entirely by air, and that the West would not negotiate over the freedom of two million people.

name: The People's Republic of China Founded (1949)
teaser: After a century of collapse, invasion, and civil war, Mao Zedong proclaimed a new China from the Gate of Heavenly Peace. Within a decade his land reforms and famines would claim tens of millions of lives.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the Communists won a civil war against a government fatally weakened by corruption and inflation, and how the new state promised land to the peasants who carried it to power. Notice the tragedy that followed: the same state's Great Leap Forward produced history's deadliest famine within a decade of its founding day.

name: The Korean War (1950-1953)
teaser: North Korea invaded the South, and within months a UN coalition and Chinese volunteers fought to a standstill along a border that had existed for five years. It's called the Forgotten War - but it never formally ended.
byline: The UN coalition vs. North Korea and China

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the war went from near-defeat to near-victory to stalemate in eighteen months, and how a single landing at Inchon turned it around. Notice the unfinished business: the armistice of 1953 was signed without a peace treaty, which is why the two Koreas are still technically at war today.

name: The First Ascent of Everest (1953)
teaser: Edmund Hillary, a New Zealand beekeeper, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa who'd survived six earlier attempts, reached the top of the world - 8,849 meters - and stayed 15 minutes. One of them relieved himself on the summit.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the pair reached the summit after a rival Swiss team had come within 100 meters the year before, and how Tenzing had already been higher than any human in history on failed expeditions. Notice the mundane detail that underlines the achievement: they spent only 15 minutes on top, out of oxygen, before starting the dangerous descent.

name: The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955-1956)
teaser: After Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat, Black residents of Montgomery walked, carpooled, and organized for 381 days until the buses integrated. The boycott's 26-year-old leader became the face of a movement.
byline: Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King Jr.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the boycott worked because Black riders were two-thirds of the bus company's customers - a community could hurt a business by walking. Notice the detail that reframes the story: Parks was a trained activist, not a tired seamstress, and her arrest was the planned test case the movement had been waiting for.

name: Sputnik Launches (1957)
teaser: A beach-ball-sized satellite beeping from orbit shocked the world and started the space race. The US, caught flat-footed, created NASA and poured billions into science education - all because of a 58-centimeter metal sphere.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the satellite was essentially a radio transmitter in a polished ball, launched by a missile designed to deliver a hydrogen bomb. Notice the panic it caused: Americans feared Soviet missiles over their heads, and Congress rushed through the law that created NASA within a year.

name: The Cuban Revolution (1959)
teaser: A bearded lawyer and 80 guerrillas in the mountains toppled a US-backed dictator who had a 30,000-man army. Within two years Castro allied with the USSR, and a revolution that promised democracy delivered one-party rule.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Castro's tiny force survived ambushes and defections, then watched Batista's army collapse from within in a few days - a revolution won more by the regime's rot than the rebels' strength. Notice the path not taken: Castro visited Washington seeking aid in April 1959; a year later Cuba was communist and the missiles crisis was four years away.

name: The Berlin Wall (1961-1989)
teaser: In one night, East Germany sealed Berlin with barbed wire, then a concrete wall with watchtowers and a 'death strip.' It stood for 28 years - the most visible wound of the Cold War - and its fall became the symbol of its end.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the wall wasn't built to keep enemies out but citizens in - 3.6 million East Germans had already fled through Berlin. Notice the human detail: at least 140 people died trying to cross, while at the same time East Germany's athletes were winning Olympic medals by being allowed to defect for the good of the state.

name: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)
teaser: For thirteen days the world stood at the edge of nuclear war over missiles 90 miles from Florida. The two leaders - one recovering from a fever, the other furious at being caught - resolved it with a secret trade no one admitted for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how U-2 photos of missile sites in Cuba started a crisis that brought the two superpowers to a naval blockade, then to a secret deal: the US quietly removed missiles from Turkey in exchange for the Soviet withdrawal. Notice how close it was: a Soviet submarine commander, cut off from orders, had to be talked out of launching a nuclear torpedo.

name: The March on Washington (1963)
teaser: A quarter of a million people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial, and Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech from steps where his voice carried over a sea of faces. It was the largest demonstration in American history up to that point.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the march was planned to pressure Congress to pass civil rights legislation, and how King's famous speech wasn't his prepared text - the 'I have a dream' refrain came from a moment of improvisation, echoing a sermon he'd given in Detroit. Notice who wasn't in the official photos: the women who organized much of it were kept off the platform.

name: The Civil Rights Act (1964)
teaser: The most sweeping civil rights law since Reconstruction outlawed segregation in public places and discrimination in employment. It passed after the longest filibuster in Senate history - 75 days.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the bill needed a two-thirds vote to break a filibuster led by southern senators who talked for weeks, and how the president's arm-twisting and a religious coalition pushed it through. Notice the law's reach: it banned the discrimination that had closed lunch counters, theaters, and hiring lines to Black Americans - and its voting protections seeded the Voting Rights Act the next year.

name: The Cultural Revolution (1966-1976)
teaser: Mao Zedong unleashed students against teachers, officials, and 'old thinking' - libraries burned, schools closed, and an estimated million people died or were driven to suicide. Mao called it 'a great disorder under heaven.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Mao, worried he was losing power, told millions of teenagers to 'bombard the headquarters,' turning classrooms into revolutionary tribunals. Notice the scale of erasure: temples, books, and centuries of artifacts were destroyed - and the chaos only stopped when the army was called in to suppress the very youth Mao had armed with slogans.

name: Apollo 11 (1969)
teaser: A computer with less power than a calculator guided three men to the moon, and 600 million people - a fifth of humanity - watched Armstrong step off the ladder. The whole program, from start to moon, took eight years.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the landing computer had 4KB of memory and ran out of processing time at the critical moment, and how Armstrong had to take manual control to find a clear landing zone with 30 seconds of fuel left. Notice the human detail: the 'one small step' was improvised, and the flag's ripple was just the aluminum pole it hung from.

name: Woodstock (1969)
teaser: A planned festival for 50,000 drew 400,000 people to a dairy farm; the organizers lost millions, the roads jammed for miles, and the music - Hendrix, Joplin, the Who - became the soundtrack of a generation. The farm's owner charged nothing for the land.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the festival had no fences, no tickets, and three births, and how helicopters ferried performers in when the roads clogged. Notice the scale of the myth-making: most of the famous performances happened late - Hendrix played Monday morning to 30,000 stragglers, and the film made it look like a million watched.

name: Watergate (1972-1974)
teaser: A third-rate burglary at a hotel office building grew into the scandal that forced the first presidential resignation in American history. It ended not with a coup but with a subpoena, a tape recorder, and 70 subpoenaed witnesses.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the break-in at the Democratic headquarters might have been forgotten - until the White House tried to cover it up, and the cover-up was caught on Nixon's own taping system, installed for his memoirs. Notice the reporter's method: two Washington Post journalists followed the money - 'follow the money' - through laundered checks to the Committee to Re-elect the President.

name: The Yom Kippur War (1973)
teaser: On Judaism's holiest day, Egypt and Syria attacked Israel by surprise. After three weeks, Israel survived - but the war shattered its invincibility myth and led, eventually, to peace with Egypt, the first Arab state to recognize it.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the attackers chose Yom Kippur precisely because the country would be empty and radio silence absolute, and how a tank war on two fronts nearly broke Israel before the US airlift turned it. Notice the war's quiet dividend: the oil embargo it triggered quadrupled oil prices, and the shock made the superpowers push for the very negotiations that produced the Egypt-Israel peace treaty.

name: The Fall of Saigon (1975)
teaser: As North Vietnamese tanks rolled in, Americans evacuated in a frantic helicopter lift from rooftops - the last helicopter left from the embassy roof with 11 Marines still waiting. The Vietnam War ended after 20 years and 3 million Vietnamese deaths.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the final evacuation carried 7,000 people out in a day, with helicopters pushed off carrier decks into the sea to make room for more, and how the embassy roof scramble became the war's defining image. Notice the numbers that framed the American debate for decades: 58,000 US dead against more than a million Vietnamese.

name: The Iran Hostage Crisis (1979-1981)
teaser: After the Iranian revolution, students seized the US embassy and held 52 Americans for 444 days - a crisis that ran through an election, a rescue failure, and ended hours after Reagan's inauguration. The students had a photographer documenting every moment for the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the takeover began as a three-day protest and became a political weapon after the Ayatollah endorsed it, and how a rescue mission died in the desert when helicopters collided. Notice the coincidence that ended it: the hostages were released minutes after the new president took office, in a deal that had secretly been in the works for months.

name: The Fall of the Berlin Wall (1989)
teaser: A spokesman's slip of the tongue - saying travel restrictions were lifted 'immediately' - sent tens of thousands to the wall, and the guards, outnumbered, opened the gates. Within a year, Germany was one country.

exploreAction.targetName: The fall of the Berlin Wall
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the wall fell because of a mistranslated press conference: the announcement was meant for the next day, and the guards had no orders for a crowd that had already reached the gates. Notice the smaller revolutions behind it: the wall fell because Hungary opened its border months earlier, and Poland and Hungary had already held the first free elections in the Soviet bloc.

name: Nelson Mandela Released (1990)
teaser: After 27 years in prison - including hard labor on Robben Island - a man walked out and, four years later, became his country's president. His release was broadcast to a world that had made his face a symbol.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years on a tiny island cell, and how the apartheid government, trying to break him, instead gave him the moral authority that ended it. Notice the detail that shows his strategy: he walked out holding his wife's hand and raised his fist, then began negotiating with the very ministers who'd jailed him.

name: The End of Apartheid (1994)
teaser: South Africa's first multiracial election, won by Nelson Mandela, ended 46 years of legalized segregation. The miracle was that the transition happened at all - with a Truth and Reconciliation Commission instead of a bloodbath.
byline: Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk

exploreAction.instruction: Read how a system that classified every citizen by race at birth was dismantled at the ballot box - 19 million people voted, most for the first time, standing in lines that snaked for miles. Notice the invention that followed: a truth commission that traded amnesty for confession, the model for a dozen post-conflict nations since.

name: The Rwandan Genocide (1994)
teaser: In 100 days, an estimated 800,000 Tutsi were killed with machetes and guns while the world's peacekeepers were ordered to stand down. The killing was planned, and the radio stations that incited it were never silenced.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how the genocide began hours after a plane crash killed the president, and how Hutu Power radio broadcast the locations of Tutsi families hiding in churches. Notice the international failure documented in chilling detail: 2,500 UN peacekeepers were on the ground, and their commander was ordered not to intervene with the 5,000 soldiers he'd requested.

name: The Channel Tunnel Opens (1994)
